solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Feature of pretty close inspections

blocks.note: "pretty" is the adjective standing for an attractive person; what marks them out is an attractive appearance
examining something carefully, a long hard stare at it

explanation.surface: It reads like a line about how attractive something looks when you examine it up close.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pretty close" wants to be one phrase meaning fairly near; the split falls after "pretty", which is the attractive person, not the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase has two senses: attractiveness, which is what makes someone pretty, and careful glances, which is what close inspections are.

clue.text: Pass on advice to young man

blocks.note: pass on is the euphemism for dying; the answer is an older slang phrase for the same thing
a famous nineteenth-century American slogan urging young men to seek their fortune on the frontier

explanation.surface: Someone is relaying a piece of advice to a youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pass on" looks like handing advice along; it is the euphemism for dying. The second half quotes the slogan "Go west, young man".
explanation.definitionFit: Go west is First World War slang for being killed, and the same words complete the pioneer-era slogan the clue half-quotes.

clue.text: Tennis star, really big, with alias

blocks.note: OS = outsize, the clothing-label abbreviation for very large
aka = also known as, which introduces an alias

explanation.surface: A description of a huge tennis star who plays under another name.
explanation.walkthrough: Naomi Osaka is a Japanese tennis champion; the city of the same name is a decoy the definition steers away from.
explanation.definitionFit: Naomi Osaka has won several Grand Slam singles titles, a definition by example.

clue.text: Those inclined to offer shares?

blocks.note: the surface offers generous people, willing to do something; a ship that lists is inclined in the other sense, leaning over
not sharing out sweets but selling stock, which only businesses on an exchange can do

explanation.surface: People who are willing to share things with others.
explanation.walkthrough: "Inclined" reads as willing; the answer takes it literally, since leaning over is listing. The question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A listed company has its shares traded on a stock exchange, and listed also means tilted, so the clue fits both ways.

clue.text: No overnight case

blocks.note: the surface suggests travelling light; the real sense is not staying the night somewhere
not a suitcase but a medical case, someone being treated

explanation.surface: Travelling without an overnight bag.
explanation.walkthrough: "Overnight case" suggests luggage; "case" is the medical sense, a patient.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpatient is treated at a hospital without being admitted overnight.

clue.text: Thus see unaided

blocks.note: so = thus
lo = see!, as in "lo and behold"

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at something with the naked eye.
explanation.walkthrough: "See unaided" reads as naked-eye viewing, but "see" belongs to the wordplay and "unaided" stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a solo flight or effort is made without help.

clue.text: Small jug that one shouldn’t drink from

definitions.text: Small jug that one shouldn’t drink from

blocks.note: S = small, as on a clothing label
a ewer is a large water jug

explanation.surface: A warning about a little jug that is not for drinking out of.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is just "Small jug"; the whole clue then describes the answer too, a channel of liquid you must never drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer carries waste water, the last thing anyone should drink, and its name is a small letter plus a jug.

clue.text: Money received by crook?

blocks.note: an income, some payment coming in
the surface offers a criminal; in Australian and British slang crook also means unwell

explanation.surface: A criminal's takings.
explanation.walkthrough: "Crook" poses as a criminal but is the slang for ill. Sickness benefit was the UK state payment to people off work through illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Sickness benefit is money the state pays to someone too ill to work, which a crook person would receive.

clue.text: Scratched and pinched

blocks.note: the racing term for a horse pulled out of a race before it starts
a pinched face is thin and drawn, shrunken in on itself

explanation.surface: Someone has been clawed and nipped.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like minor injuries. "Scratched" means pulled from the field; "pinched" is a gaunt, shrunken look.
explanation.definitionFit: A scratched runner has been taken out of the race, and a pinched, retiring look is drawn inward, the two senses of the answer.

clue.text: In studies, he’d crushed ginger nuts

indicators.note: the crushed letters go in the word for studies
crushing breaks something up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: to read a subject at university is to study it
HED rearranged, placed inside READS after RE

explanation.surface: A person bashing up ginger nut biscuits between study sessions.
explanation.walkthrough: Ginger nuts are British biscuits, so the phrase reads as snack food; here "nuts" is slang for heads.
explanation.definitionFit: A "nut" is slang for a head, so ginger nuts are people with red hair.

clue.text: Repartee about bowler’s thingy

indicators.note: the wit goes round the other piece

blocks.note: repartee is quick wit
a bowler is a hat, and bowler's = bowler is, so HAT'S

explanation.surface: Banter about a cricket bowler's unnamed object.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bowler" suggests cricket; it is the hard round hat. The apostrophe-S reads as possessive but stands for "is".
explanation.definitionFit: Both are placeholder words for an object whose name escapes you.

clue.text: Latin dictionary in which “felis” is found

indicators.note: the Latin word's meaning sits in the dictionary

blocks.note: L = Latin
OED = Oxford English Dictionary
felis is Latin for cat

explanation.surface: Looking up the Latin word felis in a dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: "Latin dictionary" reads as one book; Latin is only an abbreviation, and the dictionary is an English one. The Latin word must be translated before it goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something found has been located.

clue.text: One of keys A and B will open box

indicators.note: the new letters open up the box word and sit inside it

blocks.note: to spar is to box
the ace is the A in a pack of cards
B stays as itself, following ACE inside SPAR

explanation.surface: Keys labelled A and B are needed to unlock a box.
explanation.walkthrough: The keys look like padlock keys opening a box; they are keyboard keys, and "box" is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The space bar is the long key at the bottom of a keyboard, a definition by example.

clue.text: Wound up performing at the Fringe?

blocks.note: wound up = tense, nervous
on = performing; a fringe is a border

explanation.surface: An anxious comedian doing a show at the Edinburgh Fringe.
explanation.walkthrough: The Edinburgh Fringe is the city's huge summer arts festival. The question mark warns that the second half is read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervy and tense is one sense; the other takes the words literally, performing (on) at a border (edge).

clue.text: Promise of union action

blocks.note: the union is a marriage, and this is the promise to marry
military action, a battle

explanation.surface: A trade union's pledge to strike.
explanation.walkthrough: "Union action" reads as industrial action; the union is a marriage and the action is a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a betrothal and a clash between armed forces.

clue.text: Devout cardinal isn’t bad for Christian settlement

indicators.note: bad letters are in the wrong order

blocks.note: pi = pious, devout
CARDINALISNT rearranged

explanation.surface: A religious remark about a pious cardinal and a Christian community.
explanation.walkthrough: "Christian" is Fletcher Christian, who led the Bounty mutineers to settle the island in 1790, not the faith the cardinal suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitcairn Island was settled by Fletcher Christian and the Bounty mutineers, whose descendants still live there.

clue.text: Largely popular officer

blocks.note: in = fashionable, popular
a general is a senior army officer

explanation.surface: A well-liked officer, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: "Largely" can look like a comment on the officer's size; it is an adverb meaning mostly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean for the most part.

clue.text: We had to include gag — sorry

indicators.note: one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: we had = we'd
to gag is to retch

explanation.surface: An apology for a joke that had to go into a show.
explanation.walkthrough: "Gag" looks like a joke; it is the throat's heave. "Sorry" is not an apology but the adjective, as in a sorry sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorry in the sense of pitiful: a sorry state is a miserable, pitiable one.

clue.text: Soldier and mad outlaw in communist military group

indicators.note: the three pieces sit inside the communist

blocks.note: a red is a communist
GI = an American soldier
mental = mad, informally
to outlaw is to ban

explanation.surface: A deranged soldier and a bandit hiding in a communist army unit.
explanation.walkthrough: "Outlaw" poses as a bandit; it is the verb. "Military group" sounds like troops, but the group here plays music.
explanation.definitionFit: A regimental band is the musical group attached to an army regiment.

clue.text: Firm support — it turns out the same

blocks.note: Co. = company, a firm
a pier is a supporting pillar

explanation.surface: Steady backing that ends up unchanged.
explanation.walkthrough: "Turns out" means produces, as a machine turns out work, not "proves to be".
explanation.definitionFit: A copier churns out pages identical to the original, a cryptic description rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Polynesian in trouble, not coming back

indicators.note: the letters return the way they came, right to left

blocks.note: to nag is to trouble, to pester
not as itself

explanation.surface: A Pacific islander in difficulty, never returning.
explanation.walkthrough: "In trouble" looks like a phrase; "in" is only a link and "trouble" is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is a Polynesian kingdom in the South Pacific, so its people are Polynesians.

clue.text: Age hidden by fat old painter

indicators.note: the age is covered by the fat, so sits inside it

blocks.note: an eon is an age
lard is pig fat
O = old

explanation.surface: An elderly overweight artist whose years are disguised by his bulk.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fat old painter" reads as one unkind description; "old" is only the letter on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci is the Renaissance painter of the Mona Lisa, a definition by example.

clue.text: Monarch playing party piece?

blocks.note: R = rex or regina, king or queen
on = playing, performing
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A king doing his party piece.
explanation.walkthrough: "Party piece" is one phrase in the surface; "party" goes to the wordplay and "piece" alone is the musical composition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical piece with a recurring main theme, a definition by example.

clue.text: A winner, but no married bloke

indicators.note: the married letter is taken away

blocks.note: a champ is a winner
M = married, removed from CHAMP

explanation.surface: A victorious man who is still single.
explanation.walkthrough: M for married is the genealogical abbreviation. Bloke is British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are informal British words for a man.

clue.text: Not so easy to fit copper into grating

indicators.note: fitting something in places it inside
names the word the copper goes inside

blocks.note: a grating voice is harsh
a copper is a policeman: DI = Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: Squeezing a piece of copper metal through a grate is tricky.
explanation.walkthrough: "Copper" and "grating" read as metalwork; one is a police officer and the other an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The -ish ending softens hard to fairly hard, which is the understated not so easy.

clue.text: Mr F Ward, Independent

blocks.note: EF is the spelt-out name of the letter F
to ward off is to fend off
I = independent

explanation.surface: A name tag for an independent politician called F Ward.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is laid out like a ballot paper listing a candidate, so "Mr F Ward" looks like one name; "Mr" alone is the definition and "Ward" is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi is a Turkish and Middle Eastern courtesy title for a man, used much as Mr is.

clue.text: Valleys in feudal estates

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words

blocks.note: the run starts after FEU and stops before TATES

explanation.surface: Valleys that were once parts of a lord's lands.
explanation.walkthrough: The dales, as in the Yorkshire Dales, are the valleys of northern England; the surface reaches for medieval landholding to hide them.
explanation.definitionFit: Dale is the northern English word for a valley.

clue.text: Dainty little Parisian quartet

blocks.note: the French word for little
a quartet is four

explanation.surface: Four refined little French musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: "Dainty" looks like an adjective but is the noun: a dainty is a small delicacy.
explanation.definitionFit: A petit four is a tiny fancy cake served after dinner, exactly the sort of delicacy called a dainty.
